demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Mr. Ali, a 78-year-old Middle Eastern man and retired environmental scientist, sought help for symptoms that had been troubling him since an accident at work five years ago. On that fateful day, while working in a laboratory handling hazardous chemicals, Mr. Ali accidentally spilled a highly reactive solution onto his colleague’s face, causing severe burns. This traumatic event has left deep psychological scars that continue to affect his daily life. Mr. Ali often finds himself triggered by seemingly innocuous sounds and situations. The heavy breathing of people around him, especially in crowded areas like the grocery store or at social gatherings, reminds him of his colleague's desperate gasps for air after the accident. Each time he hears these sounds, it feels as if he is being transported back to that moment when everything went wrong. He describes feeling like the event is happening right now, and he vividly recalls the intense fear and helplessness he felt then. Feeling happy or relaxed also triggers Mr. Ali’s memories of the accident. During a recent family gathering where everyone was laughing and enjoying each other's company, Mr. Ali found himself overwhelmed by an intrusive memory of his colleague in pain. This feeling is so strong that it makes him question whether the event truly happened as he remembers it. He says, "The memory is so extreme it feels hard to believe it actually happened to me." The joy and happiness around him starkly contrasts with the trauma he experienced, creating a dissonance that intensifies his distress. Physical affection, such as hugs from his wife or children, also triggers these memories. Mr. Ali has come to associate such expressions of love with a sense of guilt and responsibility for his colleague’s injuries. He remembers the accident in vivid detail, yet struggles to articulate the emotions it evokes. "I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it," he explains. The act of receiving affection brings him back to that moment of pain and suffering, making it difficult for him to fully engage in these moments with his loved ones. Over time, Mr. Ali has noticed that certain triggers consistently lead to reliving the event. Each instance where heavy breathing or expressions of happiness occur seems to set off a chain reaction in which he is transported back to the laboratory. These memories feel so immediate and intense that they overshadow any present moment joy or comfort. As a result, his relationships with family members have been strained, as he has become increasingly withdrawn during times when they are trying to enjoy each other’s company. Mr. Ali's occupation as an environmental scientist has also been affected by these symptoms. He recalls feeling particularly vulnerable while working in the lab after the accident. The sounds of breathing and machinery would often trigger memories that made it difficult for him to focus on his work. Despite retiring a few years ago, he still feels haunted by these experiences. What finally brought Mr. Ali to seek help was the realization that his symptoms were becoming increasingly debilitating. He was certain that he could no longer ignore the intense distress and guilt he felt every day. His primary fear is that he will never be able to move past this event, but he also hopes for a way to reconcile these memories with his present life and find peace. In conclusion, Mr. Ali's narrative reveals how triggers such as heavy breathing sounds, feelings of happiness, and physical affection lead directly to reliving the traumatic event. The vividness and intensity of these memories have left him struggling to engage in daily activities and maintain relationships, highlighting the urgent need for therapeutic intervention.
